subject.name: BASS-II (PSI-25)

insights.text: BASS-II (PSI-25) burned thin PMMA sheets (0.1 to 0.4 mm thick, 1 to 2 cm wide) aboard the ISS in microgravity with an opposed airflow [BASS2-TM]. In several runs the flame spread steadily and then went out as the flow was turned down [PSI25-B10, PSI25-B21, PSI25-B22], in one run it went out quickly after the flow was stopped [PSI25-B1], and other samples blew out at high fan settings [PSI25-B18, PSI25-B19]. For a lunar habitat or rover this makes cabin airflow a fire lever: very low flow starved these flames in microgravity, while a cabin on the Moon also has weak buoyant flow that these 0 g tests did not include. These rows are draft: their oxygen values are initial and final chamber readings and the fan settings are uncalibrated, so no oxygen or flow limit is taken from them [PSI25-B6, PSI25-B11, PSI25-B12, PSI25-B13, PSI25-B14, PSI25-B15, PSI25-B16, PSI25-B17, PSI25-B20].

subject.name: NASA 2025 solid fuel ignition testing for lunar applications

insights.text: NASA's 2025 lunar-application tests measured the oxygen level at which six materials went out within a 5 s drop at simulated lunar gravity and 56.5 kPa (8.2 psia) [US25]. The reported levels run from 11% O2 for cotton fabric [U25-03-L, U25-04-L], 13% for P213 tape [U25-02-L] and 13.5% for PMMA [U25-01-L] up to 21% for polycarbonate [U25-05-L] and 24% for Nomex Velcro [U25-06-L]. The 34% O2 of the 8.2 psia exploration atmosphere preset is above every one of these measured extinction levels [exploration-8.2-34], so material choice for a lunar cabin at that atmosphere cannot rely on these materials going out on their own. These are simulated-gravity results under scientific review, read from plots, and one cotton value is a smolder endpoint, so treat them as close-to-limit evidence rather than an on-Moon rating.

insights.text: Olson and Ferkul (2012) compared Nomex HT90-40 fabric at 101.3 kPa (14.7 psia) in Earth gravity, simulated lunar gravity and microgravity with forced flow [OF12]. The low-gravity and 1 g pass criteria differ, so these are close-to-limit indicators across gravity, not a one-to-one comparison.

subject.name: MIST: Material Ignition and Suppression Test in space exploration atmospheres

insights.text: The MIST project reported an approximate limiting oxygen concentration for flame spread over a 12.7 mm black PMMA rod with opposed flow of about 18.8% O2 in a 1 g ground test and about 16.2% O2 aboard the ISS, both near 100 kPa [M25-FS-G, M25-FS-M]. The lower microgravity value means this material kept a flame at less oxygen in orbit than on the ground, so a ground test alone could understate the fire risk in a spacecraft. For a lunar base, where gravity lies between these cases, the 0 g and 1 g values only bound an estimate; no lunar measurement is in these rows. Flow speed, heating and uncertainty for this pair are unresolved, so both values are draft [M25].

subject.name: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS)

insights.text: BASS (PSI-26) burned cotton/fiberglass, Nomex and Ultem fabric sheets, spheres and cylinders aboard the ISS in microgravity, varying airflow speed and direction, material and geometry, and the use of nitrogen as a suppressant [bass, PSI-26]. The reported test conditions ran from 17% to 21% O2 at 101.3 kPa [guide]. Early tests showed that a nitrogen jet could strengthen a flame by pulling in surrounding oxygen [guide]. For suppression in a lunar base or pressurized rover, an inert-gas discharge aimed at a fire therefore needs to be checked for this effect rather than assumed to put the flame out. These are microgravity results, and the catalog does not establish their transfer to lunar gravity.

subject.name: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX)

For suppression and detection in a lunar base or pressurized rover, the end of a visible flame is therefore not a reliable sign that a liquid-fuel fire has stopped reacting.
